intro: Read the deck for the content and these notes for the thinking. Each note explains a slide, gives you a way to remember it or warns you where fundraisers slip. Work the examples in pencil, answer the recall questions with the page covered, and write your own marginal notes beside mine.

sections.title: What Fundraising Really Is
sections.big_idea: Fundraising is **resource mobilisation**: the mission leads, money follows, and relationships matter more than any single transaction.
in_plain_words: Fundraising secures the money, goods, skills and goodwill an organisation needs for its mission. Money is one resource among several, and volunteers, donated space and board introductions count too. The chain runs mission, strategy, resources, fundraising. Reverse it and you drift toward whatever is fundable.

Treat donors as partners. Report, thank and involve them, and track the retention rate alongside income, because an organisation replacing all its donors each year is running to stand still. Fundraising belongs to everyone, from the finance lead to the director. The long goal is a **resilient base** that survives losing any single funder.

nodes.label: Mission
nodes.sub: the change you exist to create

diagram.caption: the healthy order; reverse it and mission drift follows

key_terms.meaning: Acquiring the financial and non-financial resources a mission needs.
Moving away from your focus one fundable grant at a time.
The share of donors who give again.
Goods, equipment, space and pro-bono services given instead of cash.
The share of income from your largest funder.
Shared running costs such as salaries, systems and audits.

worked_example.title: Why retention beats finding new donors
worked_example.setup: Illustrative: last year you had 200 donors and this year 120 of them gave again.
steps: Donors who did not renew: 200 − 120 = 80.
Retention rate: 120 ÷ 200 = 0.6, which is 60 percent.
To keep 200 donors next year you must find 80 new ones to replace the lost donors.
Each extra donor you keep reduces the number you must acquire.
worked_example.answer: 60 percent retention, and 80 donors to replace just to stand still.

mistakes: Treating fundraising as begging. Apologetic asks lead to underselling the budget.
Ignoring non-cash resources. Volunteer time, donated space and pro-bono work are resources, and uncounted ones leave you looking smaller than you are.
Dismissing overheads as waste. Salaries, systems and audits are what make impact deliverable and auditable.
Relying on one big donor. Dependence on a single funder is the fastest route to an organisational crisis.

recall.q: What is the healthy sequence from mission to money?
recall.a: Mission, strategy, resources, fundraising.

recall.q: Name three kinds of resource an organisation mobilises.
recall.a: Money, in-kind goods and services, and people (volunteers, skills, networks).

recall.q: Name two things a donor receives in return for a gift.
recall.a: Any two of: a share in the change, meaning, recognition, tax benefit, confidence it was used well.

recall.q: Which two numbers measure whether a funding base is building?
recall.a: The concentration ratio and the unrestricted share.

recall.q: Why is the finance lead called the most under-recognised fundraiser?
recall.a: A late utilisation certificate can end renewals that good programme work cannot recover.

sections.title: The Funding Picture
sections.big_idea: Each source has its own logic and cost. **Restricted money from a few sources** leaves you little to decide for yourself.
in_plain_words: NGO income comes from foundation grants, government schemes and contracts, CSR, individual gifts, crowdfunding and earned income. Grants are large but restricted and time-limited. Government pays slowly. CSR is statutory and tied to Schedule VII with a March pressure point. Individual giving is slow to build and unrestricted.

Look at the restricted column. An organisation funded entirely from grants, government and CSR has almost no money it can decide how to spend. Crowdfunding finds first-time donors but the platform usually holds the relationship. Earned income can grow with you but needs tax checks. **No single slice should dominate.**

key_terms.meaning: Money tied to a project or line item that you must spend as agreed.
Money you decide how to allocate, including overheads.
Government grants, often released slowly with payment arrears.
The list of activities CSR money may be spent on.
Many small online gifts around one urgent, time-bound story.
Income-tax registration; earned income can put it at risk if mishandled.

worked_example.title: Read an illustrative funding mix
worked_example.setup: Illustrative: an NGO with income of 100 lakh. Foundation grants 55, CSR 20, individuals 15, earned income 10.
steps: Check the mix adds up: 55 + 20 + 15 + 10 = 100.
Share of the largest source: 55 ÷ 100 = 0.55, or 55 percent.
Unrestricted income from individuals and earned income: 15 + 10 = 25.
Unrestricted share: 25 ÷ 100 = 0.25, or 25 percent.
Ask which slice would hurt most if it vanished.
worked_example.answer: The largest source is 55 percent and the unrestricted share is 25 percent.

mistakes: Treating CSR as a variety of grant. The constraints come from statute and are not negotiable.
Taking government work you cannot pre-finance. The structural risk is payment delay.
Assuming a successful crowdfunding campaign gives you a donor base. Without captured contact details and permission, you have money and no base.
Ignoring the CSR March deadline. A proposal in January is received differently from one in June.

recall.q: Which source is usually unrestricted and slow to build?
recall.a: Individual giving.

recall.q: When does the CSR cycle peak?
recall.a: March, at the end of the financial year.

recall.q: What is the main structural risk in government funding?
recall.a: Payment delay, so you may fund the scheme from your own reserves for months.

recall.q: Name two platforms for crowdfunding in India.
recall.a: Any two of: Ketto, Milaap, GiveIndia, DonateKart.

recall.q: What is the test the deck gives for earned income?
recall.a: Would the activity exist if it made no money?

sections.title: Knowing Your Donors
sections.big_idea: Institutions move on **evidence and alignment**, individuals on **story and trust**. Each donor asks five silent questions.
in_plain_words: Institutional donors decide by committee against criteria, give large restricted sums and move on a formal cycle. Individuals decide on feeling and trust, give smaller sums, often unrestricted. The skills do not transfer. Donors give for belief, trust, identity, connection and the ask of someone they trust.

Every donor asks why this cause, why this organisation, why now, why me, and how will I know. Money also carries power: the funder sets themes, formats and timelines while the grantee knows the community. Vet the donor too, decide your red lines early, and **segment donors** so each gets the right message.

key_terms.meaning: Grouping donors by giving level, channel, loyalty and interest.
The core document answering why your cause deserves funding.
Funders set the agenda; grantees hold the local knowledge.
Checking a donor's sources and conditions before accepting money.
Conditions you decide in advance you will refuse.
Funds the funder decides how to spend; most Indian NGO money.

worked_example.title: Match donors to segments
worked_example.setup: Use the slide 29 table to assign a message and channel to four donors.
steps: A first-time ₹500 online giver: a warm thank-you and proof of use, by email or WhatsApp.
A monthly donor: regular contact and rarely an ask, by email or an occasional call.
A major donor: personal attention from leadership, in person.
A CSR head: compliance evidence and a site visit, in a meeting.
Check each message answers the donor's five questions.
worked_example.answer: Four different messages and channels; the same mass appeal underperforms for each.

mistakes: Pitching a foundation like a friend, or a friend like a logframe. The skills do not transfer.
Writing a case that cannot answer 'why now'. Giving can then be deferred indefinitely.
Reporting a single income figure. It hides whether you have any money you can decide about.
Deciding your red lines when an offer is on the table. Refusing a specific offer that would fund three salaries is hard.

recall.q: What are the five questions a donor asks?
recall.a: Why this cause, why this organisation, why now, why me, and how will I know it worked?

recall.q: What is the usual real reason behind much giving?
recall.a: Being asked by someone they trust.

recall.q: Which funds cover overheads and build reserves?
recall.a: Unrestricted funds.

recall.q: Name two distortions caused by the funder-grantee imbalance.
recall.a: Any two of: chasing fashionable themes, reporting crowding out delivery, short cycles blocking long work, indicators shaping the programme.

recall.q: How many segments does the slide 29 table list?
recall.a: Five: first-time giver, monthly donor, major donor, CSR head and institutional funder.

sections.title: Strategy & the Fundraising Cycle
sections.big_idea: The ask is **one moment in a long cycle**. Cultivation and stewardship cost little and decide whether the gift happens twice.
in_plain_words: A fundraising strategy replaces the scramble with a plan: how much you need, from which sources, by when and who is responsible, plus what you will decline. The case for support is the document you write once and adapt. Prospect research finds funders whose theme, geography, typical grant size and openness match you.

Then run the cycle: identify, cultivate, ask, steward and renew. Cultivation builds trust before the ask, and being honest about a setback buys more credibility than a success story. Make a specific ask, **then stop talking**. Stewardship is where the next gift is earned, and the pyramid shows donors moving upward over time.

key_terms.meaning: A plan stating need, sources, targets, owners and what you will decline.
Problem, solution, evidence, what a gift makes possible and the cost of inaction.
Finding donors whose interests, geography and giving size match yours.
Building a relationship before any request.
Everything you do after the gift: thanks, reports and contact.
Many small donors at the base, a few major and legacy donors at the top.

worked_example.title: Check the size fit before you apply
worked_example.setup: Illustrative: a funder's median past grant is 5 lakh, and you were about to ask for 50 lakh.
steps: Your ask against their median: 50 ÷ 5 = 10 times.
A tenfold ask shows you did not check, however good the thematic fit.
Redesign: ask for 12 lakh over two years, which is 12 ÷ 2 = 6 lakh a year.
Against the median: 6 ÷ 5 = 1.2 times, close to their typical size.
Add a clear next step, such as sending the full proposal by Friday.
worked_example.answer: The 50 lakh ask is 10 times their median; a 12 lakh two-year ask is 1.2 times a year.

mistakes: Moving straight to the ask. Cultivation decides whether it succeeds, and it is the stage most often skipped.
Filling the silence after the ask. You end up negotiating against yourself.
Reporting only successes. A mixed result reported in full is survivable, while one discovered later is not.
Cultivating indefinitely because asking is uncomfortable. Set the date you will ask by.

recall.q: What are the five stages of the cycle?
recall.a: Identify, cultivate, ask, steward and renew.

recall.q: Which two stages are most often skipped?
recall.a: Cultivation and stewardship.

recall.q: Name three things to check in prospect research.
recall.a: Any three of: theme, geography, typical grant size, organisations like you, whether they are open.

recall.q: What are the three parts of a strong ask?
recall.a: A clear amount, a clear purpose and a defined next step.

recall.q: What is the rule for the most valuable cultivation signal?
recall.a: Be honest about a setback, because it buys more credibility than success stories.

sections.title: Writing a Winning Proposal
sections.big_idea: A proposal is **logic made visible**: problem, change, budget and measurement that all agree with each other.
in_plain_words: Seven sections do the work: problem statement, objectives, theory of change, activities, M&E, budget and sustainability. Open with the problem instead of your organisation, and give evidence for who is affected and why it persists. Objectives describe change. Train 200 teachers is an activity, while improved Grade 3 reading in 40 schools is an outcome.

A logframe runs from inputs to impact. You control the first three levels, partly control outcomes and barely control impact, yet funders judge you on outcomes. Count outputs as outputs. Plan an indicator, a baseline, a target and a budget line, name a real exit mechanism, **follow the format exactly** and have someone outside the sector read it.

key_terms.meaning: What you produce, such as 500 women trained.
What changes as a result, such as incomes rising.
A grid of levels, indicators and assumptions.
The reasoning for why each arrow in the logic should hold.
The starting measurement; it cannot be recovered later.
Specific, Measurable, Achievable, Relevant, Time-bound.

worked_example.title: Run a pre-submission check
worked_example.setup: A draft promises 40 villages in the narrative, and its budget costs 12 villages. One objective reads 'Teachers using the method in class'.
steps: Villages with no money behind them: 40 − 12 = 28.
Share of the narrative the budget covers: 12 ÷ 40 = 0.3, or 30 percent.
Read the proposal backwards, budget first, then activities, then objectives, until both agree.
Classify the objective: teachers using the method in class is an outcome, since behaviour changed.
Check it has an indicator, a baseline, a target and a method.
worked_example.answer: A gap of 28 villages; the objective is an outcome and needs a baseline.

mistakes: Opening with your organisation. The reviewer is deciding whether to care about the problem.
Promising outputs and calling them outcomes. A reviewer reads that as not knowing the difference.
Promising impact in a three-year proposal. Promise the outcome and name the impact it contributes to.
Writing 'we will seek further funding' as the sustainability plan. Reviewers read it as an admission there is no plan.

recall.q: Which sections must a proposal contain?
recall.a: Problem statement, objectives, theory of change, activities, M&E, budget and sustainability.

recall.q: Which logframe level do funders judge you on?
recall.a: Outcomes.

recall.q: Why must the baseline be collected early?
recall.a: It cannot be retrofitted; without it you lose the ability to show what changed.

recall.q: Give one credible sustainability answer.
recall.a: Community ownership with a named mechanism, government adoption, earned income with numbers, or a benefit that needs no maintenance.

recall.q: What is the cheapest reason to reject a proposal?
recall.a: Not following the format and word limits.

sections.title: Budgeting & Financial Basics
sections.big_idea: A budget is your theory of change in money. **Cost the overhead accurately**, because under-budgeting means delivering at a loss.
in_plain_words: Funders read budgets closely. Round numbers read as estimated, no inflation reads as unconsidered and a very low overhead reads as unsustainable. Direct costs are tied to a project, indirect costs are shared. Calculate your true overhead rate once a year, state its basis and apply it to every budget.

The starvation cycle runs on both sides: funders press for low overheads, NGOs under-report and weaken their systems, and funders then see weakness. Fundraising itself costs money, and new donors cost more than renewing ones. Full cost recovery, careful co-funding and healthy numbers such as **reserves, audits and cash flow** make you fundable.

diagram.note: calculate once a year and state the basis

key_terms.meaning: Costs tied to one project, such as field staff and supplies.
Shared running costs: rent, finance, audit, IT and management.
Pricing a project to cover direct costs plus a fair share of overheads.
Pressure for low overheads that hollows out an NGO's systems.
A required share of the budget from other sources.
A funder multiplying what you raise elsewhere.

worked_example.title: Apply your overhead rate
worked_example.setup: Illustrative: shared costs are 120,000 and total direct costs are 1,000,000. A new project has direct costs of 500,000, and the funder caps overheads at 3 percent.
steps: Overhead rate: 120,000 ÷ 1,000,000 = 0.12, or 12 percent.
Overhead to charge on the new project: 500,000 × 0.12 = 60,000.
Overhead the funder will allow: 500,000 × 0.03 = 15,000.
Shortfall you must fund from elsewhere: 60,000 − 15,000 = 45,000.
Decide deliberately whether this grant is worth taking at that loss.
worked_example.answer: A 12 percent rate gives 60,000, so the 3 percent cap leaves a 45,000 shortfall.

mistakes: Padding the budget or under-budgeting it. Both damage you, padding by losing trust and under-budgeting by forcing a loss.
Inventing an overhead rate per proposal. You end up with grants that none cover actual costs.
Committing co-funding you have not secured. A funding win becomes a deadline you may miss.
Treating a 95 percent programme ratio as a selling point. Experienced funders read it as hidden overheads.

recall.q: How does the deck define the overhead rate?
recall.a: Shared costs divided by total direct costs, audited and stated with its basis.

recall.q: What is the difference between co-funding and matching?
recall.a: Co-funding means you bring a share of the budget; matching means the funder multiplies what you raise.

recall.q: What are the four steps of the starvation cycle?
recall.a: Funders pressure for low overheads, NGOs under-report, weak systems underperform and funders demand leaner overheads.

recall.q: Which numbers do funders check?
recall.a: Reserves, audited accounts, programme-to-cost ratio, cash flow and current registrations.

recall.q: Why should you be willing to decline some grants?
recall.a: Some grants cost more than they bring when overheads are not covered.

sections.title: Individual Giving & Relationships
sections.big_idea: Individual donors give **unrestricted, renewable money** and a constituency, and a small first gift is the start of a long value.
in_plain_words: Individual giving is the closest an NGO comes to independence: unrestricted income, renewal by habit and people with a stake in your survival. It is slow to build and the cost comes first. Acquiring a donor costs far more than keeping one, so lifetime value is the right measure, and retention is the highest-return activity.

Stewardship drives retention: thank within days and show the impact of their specific gift. Monthly donors give predictable, low-cost, high-retention income, and major donors need leadership time and bespoke care. Institutions respond to evidence and individuals to **one real story**, told with dignity and consent.

diagram.caption: stewardship as the road to renewal

key_terms.meaning: Total a donor is likely to give across the whole relationship.
Winning a new donor, which costs far more than keeping one.
Keeping donors giving; the highest-return activity.
Recurring gifts: predictable, low servicing cost, high retention.
A donor needing personal cultivation by leadership.
Donors lost; a monthly base needs it kept low.

worked_example.title: Lifetime value of a monthly donor
worked_example.setup: Slide 60 compares a ₹500 first-time donor who gives monthly for ten years with a one-off ₹5,000 gift.
steps: Monthly donor in one year: 500 × 12 = 6,000.
Over ten years: 6,000 × 10 = 60,000.
Compared with the one-off gift: 60,000 ÷ 5,000 = 12 times.
A ₹500 first gift looks irrational against acquisition cost, and rational against ten years of renewal.
worked_example.answer: The monthly donor is worth 60,000 over ten years, twelve times the one-off gift.

mistakes: Judging a small first gift against its acquisition cost. Lifetime value is the right comparison.
Sending a general impact report and expecting renewal. Name what the donor's specific gift paid for.
Making monthly gifts hard to cancel. It produces complaints, chargebacks and reputational damage.
Letting three major donors supply most individual income. That is single-funder dependence in a different costume.

recall.q: Why is individual giving unrestricted?
recall.a: Donors give for the mission generally, so the money can cover overheads and reserves.

recall.q: What is the phrase 'doing the work' in stewardship?
recall.a: 'Their specific gift'.

recall.q: What makes monthly donors valuable?
recall.a: Predictable income, low servicing cost, the highest retention and usually unrestricted money.

recall.q: Who should lead major-donor work?
recall.a: Leadership, since it is leadership time and not fundraising-staff time.

recall.q: Which audience is moved by one specific story?
recall.a: The individual donor, with evidence in a supporting role.

sections.title: CSR in India
sections.big_idea: CSR is a **legal duty turned into a funding stream**: predictable, annual and restricted to Schedule VII, with CSR-1 as the gate.
in_plain_words: Section 135 of the Companies Act, 2013 requires qualifying companies to spend at least 2% of their average net profit from the preceding three years on CSR. Spending is limited to Schedule VII activities, overseen by a board committee and policy. CSR cannot fund your organisation's core costs.

Prospect from public disclosures: who must spend, what they spent, on which heads and where. Under-spend is the best signal. Companies want valid registrations (CSR-1, 12A, 80G), a verifiable track record, rigorous reporting and visible outcomes. Expect the **March pressure point**, decide your co-branding position early and budget for reporting.

key_terms.meaning: The Companies Act, 2013 provision making CSR spending a legal duty.
The menu of social purposes CSR funds may be spent on.
Ministry of Corporate Affairs registration an implementing NGO needs.
Failure to spend the CSR obligation, a signal of a receptive prospect.
Companies' common preference for projects near their operations.
Public association with a company; decide your position first.

worked_example.title: How much must a company spend?
worked_example.setup: Illustrative: a qualifying company had net profits of 90, 100 and 110 crore in the preceding three years.
steps: Total of the three years: 90 + 100 + 110 = 300.
Average net profit: 300 ÷ 3 = 100 crore.
At least 2 percent must be spent: 100 × 0.02 = 2 crore.
Check Section 135 applies, and confirm current thresholds in the Act and CSR Rules.
Map your project to a Schedule VII head before you pitch.
worked_example.answer: At least 2 crore a year, spendable only on Schedule VII heads.

mistakes: Pitching CSR for general core funding. Only listed Schedule VII activities qualify.
Approaching a company without CSR-1. The conversation usually ends there.
Ignoring under-spend data. It is public and almost nobody uses it.
Spending the pitch time on documents. Offer a site visit early, since companies fund what they have seen.

recall.q: What does Section 135 require?
recall.a: Qualifying companies must spend at least 2% of average net profit of the preceding three years on CSR.

recall.q: What does Schedule VII list?
recall.a: The permitted CSR activities, from hunger and health to education, gender equality, environment and rural development.

recall.q: Which registration gives access to CSR funds at all?
recall.a: CSR-1, from the Ministry of Corporate Affairs.

recall.q: Which signal marks the most receptive CSR prospect?
recall.a: A company that under-spent its obligation last year.

recall.q: Why does the CSR cycle matter in March?
recall.a: Companies must spend by year end, so timing and readiness change how proposals are received.

sections.title: Compliance & Accountability
sections.big_idea: Registrations are **eligibility gates**: miss a filing and funding can stop overnight. Transparency then earns trust above the legal minimum.
in_plain_words: 12A/12AB exempts the NGO's income from tax if it is applied to charitable objects, and 12AB must be renewed. 80G lets donors claim a deduction, so show it on every appeal and receipt. CSR-1 opens CSR funds. FCRA governs foreign money, with a designated SBI New Delhi account and, since 2020, no sub-granting. Treat this as orientation and take legal advice.

Compliance satisfies the regulator, and transparency earns trust: publish audited accounts, an annual report and honest results, and answer to communities too. Keep one **compliance calendar** with named owners and reminders months ahead, because almost every failure in the sector is a missed date.

children.label: Donor deduction
items: State it on page and receipt

key_terms.meaning: Income-tax exemption for the NGO, renewable under the 12AB regime.
Approval letting donors claim a deduction on gifts to you.
The law governing receipt and use of foreign contributions.
Passing foreign funds to another organisation; banned from 2020.
A single list of deadlines, owners and early reminders.
Answering to the community as well as to funders.

worked_example.title: Which registrations does each offer need?
worked_example.setup: Three funding offers arrive in one month. Use the slide 75 table to list the gates for each.
steps: A company CSR grant: CSR-1 to receive it, with 12A/12AB and 80G in place.
A foreign foundation grant: valid FCRA registration or prior permission, received in the designated SBI New Delhi account, and no passing it on.
An individual appeal: 80G stated on the donation page and receipt.
Add each renewal date to the compliance calendar with a named owner and a reminder months ahead.
worked_example.answer: CSR-1 for the first, FCRA for the second and 80G for the third, all kept current by timely filings.

mistakes: Treating registrations as paperwork. They decide whether you can be funded at all.
Relying on the old 12A as permanent. Under 12AB it is renewable and a lapse creates a tax liability.
Passing on foreign funds through an intermediary. The 2020 amendment banned sub-granting.
Assuming compliance is enough. Transparency, which is voluntary and rare, is what differentiates you.

recall.q: What does 12A do, and what does 80G do?
recall.a: 12A exempts the NGO's income from tax; 80G lets donors claim a deduction.

recall.q: What are the two key changes of the FCRA amendment of 2020?
recall.a: No sub-granting, and receipt only in the designated SBI New Delhi account.

recall.q: What do the Income-tax Act 2025 section numbers refer to?
recall.a: Section 332 for 12A/12AB registration and section 354 for 80G, from 1 April 2026.

recall.q: Name three items on the compliance calendar.
recall.a: Any three of: audit and returns, FCRA returns, renewals of FCRA/80G/12AB, CSR utilisation reports, grant reports.

recall.q: Which accountability has no enforcement?
recall.a: Downward accountability to the community.

sections.title: Diversification & Sustainability
sections.big_idea: Calculate your **largest funder's share of income**. It predicts fragility better than any other number, and fixing it takes years.
in_plain_words: An organisation drawing most of its income from one funder is one decision from crisis. Diversification spreads income across grants, CSR, individuals, government and earned income. Every step takes longer than the crisis that prompts it, so start while things are fine. Reserves, built only from unrestricted income, buy time and the ability to refuse bad money.

Diversify with a plan: map your income, set a target mix, invest in what you lack, sequence one new stream at a time and review yearly. Avoid the opposite failure of dozens of tiny grants, whose reporting can cost more than they bring. Sustainability is also **capable staff, working systems and community ownership**.

key_terms.meaning: Dependence on one funder, shown by its share of your income.
Spreading income across several sources so losing one is survivable.
Unrestricted funds set aside to survive delays, losses and emergencies.
Dozens of tiny restricted grants whose compliance overhead exceeds the income.
The part of income you can allocate freely.
Map, target, invest, sequence, review.

worked_example.title: Read a concentration ratio
worked_example.setup: Illustrative: total income is 100 lakh and the largest funder gives 55 lakh. You want that funder under 30 percent.
steps: Concentration ratio: 55 ÷ 100 = 0.55, or 55 percent.
On slide 84, 40–70 percent is vulnerable, so plan the reduction.
Largest share allowed at 30 percent: 100 × 0.3 = 30 lakh.
Income to replace from other sources: 55 − 30 = 25 lakh.
The scattered trap: 30 grants of 2 lakh is 30 × 2 = 60 lakh of income, with thirty reports to write.
worked_example.answer: 55 percent, so 25 lakh must come from other sources, without creating thirty tiny grants.

mistakes: Waiting for a crisis to diversify. Every timeline is longer than the crisis.
Mistaking dozens of tiny grants for diversification. Thirty reporting cycles can use more staff time than they fund.
Starting several new streams at once. Each needs sustained attention for years.
Reading sustainability as a balanced budget. An organisation with money and no capacity is temporarily funded.

recall.q: What is the concentration ratio?
recall.a: The share of income from your largest funder.

recall.q: How much of the income from the largest funder puts you 'one decision away from crisis'?
recall.a: Over 70 percent.

recall.q: What are the five steps of a diversification plan?
recall.a: Map, target, invest, sequence and review.

recall.q: What can reserves buy?
recall.a: Surviving a delayed tranche, time to replace a funder, pre-financing and the ability to decline bad money.

recall.q: What is the test of sustainability on slide 91?
recall.a: What survives your departure.

sections.title: Ethics, Practice & Further Reading
sections.big_idea: Stories carry power over the people in them, so tell them **with dignity and real consent**, and answer to communities as well as to donors.
in_plain_words: Fundraising runs on stories, and the person in the story bears consequences you do not. Poverty porn works in the short term and corrodes trust and dignity. Real consent means comprehension: where the story appears, for how long, whether the person is named and the right to withdraw, with refusal costing nothing. Composite stories need a label.

Accountability runs two ways. Upward accountability to donors is enforced by money. **Downward accountability to the community** has no enforcement and needs a deliberate mechanism. Set ethical lines before pressure arrives and write them into a board-approved policy. Read primary sources for compliance, and calculate your own concentration ratio.

diagram.caption: the same story, told two ways

key_terms.meaning: Exploiting suffering to trigger guilt and donations while stripping dignity.
Understanding of use, venue, duration and withdrawal, freely given.
Several people merged into one case; misrepresentation unless labelled.
Reports, audits and results owed to donors.
Listening and honesty owed to the community.
Limits agreed in advance, such as no inflated numbers.

worked_example.title: Test a story before publishing
worked_example.setup: A fundraiser wants to use a mother's story and photograph in an appeal.
steps: Explain where it will appear, for how long, whether she is named and how she can withdraw.
Ask through someone with no power over her, in her language, with a real option to say no.
Check that refusal costs her nothing, or it is not consent.
Check accuracy: no staged scene and no composite passed off as one person.
Apply the practical test: would you show it to her in front of her neighbours?
worked_example.answer: Publish only if every check passes; otherwise use another story or leave it out.

mistakes: Treating a signed release as consent. The duty is to comprehension, not paperwork.
Using a composite 'typical' case without saying so.
Letting accountability to funders crowd out accountability to the people you serve.
Deciding ethical lines under pressure. Every line gets tested when crossing it funds three salaries.

recall.q: What are the five ethical lines on slide 97?
recall.a: No misleading claims, no exploiting suffering, no money whose conditions betray the mission, no pressure tactics, no misuse of donor or community data.

recall.q: What must consent cover?
recall.a: Where it appears, how long, the right to withdraw, whether they are named, and that refusal costs nothing.

recall.q: Why does downward accountability need a mechanism?
recall.a: It has no enforcement, so without a process it stays a value.

recall.q: Which number should you take from the deck?
recall.a: The share of income from your largest funder.

recall.q: What is the practical test for poverty porn?
recall.a: Would you be comfortable showing the material to the person in it, in front of their neighbours?

notes.2: Use the agenda to see the arc: what fundraising is, where money comes from, who the donors are, then strategy, proposals, budgets, individual giving, CSR and compliance, and finally diversification and ethics. If you are short of time, the five takeaways on slide 98 summarise the whole course.
notes.4: Fix the order in your mind: mission first, resources second. The framing table shows how begging, sales and resource mobilisation produce different behaviour. The slide's sharpest point is that someone who feels they are begging asks for less than the work costs. Write the full cost into every ask.
notes.5: Mission drift is the risk of reversing the chain. It arrives as a series of reasonable decisions to take grants slightly off focus, and shows only after about three years. Use the slide's test: would you still do this work if a different funder offered the same money for something else?
notes.6: Compare the two columns and decide where your organisation sits. The practical measure is retention: track the share of last year's donors who give again, alongside income. A target in rupees alone rewards finding new donors and ignores the loss of old ones.
notes.7: Count everything you mobilise. Volunteer doctors, donated space, pro-bono legal hours and a board member's introduction are all resources. Record and value them so you can show your real size to a funder, and so valued in-kind work can meet a co-funding match where the funder allows.
notes.8: Fundraising is a team job. Use the role table to see how each person feeds the case: the programme officer documents change and the finance lead delivers clean accounts. Take the slide's warning seriously. A late utilisation certificate can end a renewal that excellent programme work would otherwise secure.
notes.9: A donor receives something in return, and naming it makes an honest case. The last row decides renewal: a donor who cannot tell whether the gift achieved anything usually just stops giving. Check each row against your own reports and receipts, including your 80G status.
notes.10: Learn the myths as pairs with their corrections. The overhead myth is the most expensive because donors believe it too, and it leads to the starvation cycle later in the deck. When you answer it, be specific about what the overhead buys, such as the audit or the finance officer.
notes.11: Move from plugging this year's gap to building a base that survives losing any funder. The slide gives two numbers to track: the concentration ratio and the unrestricted share. If income grows while both ratios stay flat, the organisation is still plugging gaps.
notes.13: Map the sources before you ask anyone for money. The restricted column makes the diversification argument: an organisation funded entirely from grants, government and CSR has almost no money it can decide how to spend. Note the CSR March deadline, which changes how a January proposal is received.
notes.14: This chart is illustrative, and the slide says there is no correct split. What to take from it is that no single slice dominates. Draw your own organisation's funding mix in the same form and ask which slice would hurt most if it vanished.
notes.15: Grants are large but restricted, reporting is heavy and funding is time-limited. Plan the cliff from day one: a three-year grant that funds five staff creates a decision in month thirty. Lead time matters too, so research funders early and check their cycle before spending months on an application.
notes.16: Government money rewards compliance and reach more than a polished pitch. The structural risk is late payment, so you may fund a scheme from your own reserves for months. The rule on the slide is plain: never take government work you cannot pre-finance.
notes.17: Treat CSR as statutory partnership money that differs from a grant. The constraints come from law: Schedule VII purposes, a board committee and CSR-1 registration. Use the table to list how it differs from a grant, and read section 8 for the rules in detail.
notes.18: Individual giving is the hardest to start and the most valuable to own. The cost lands in year one and the benefit in year three, and grant budgets rarely fund year one. The trap is circular: you need unrestricted money to build the stream that produces unrestricted money.
notes.19: Crowdfunding suits a specific, urgent, time-bound story and works poorly for core costs. The main point is ownership: the relationship usually belongs to the platform. Capture contact details and permission to use them, or a successful campaign leaves you with money and no donor base.
notes.20: Earned income is unrestricted and can grow with the organisation. Treat it as one stream among several and never as a rescue plan. Use the honest test on the slide: would the activity exist if it made no money? Check the tax position and 12A/12AB implications before you scale it.
notes.22: Institutional and individual donors need different skills. Remember the pairing: evidence and alignment for institutions, story and relationship for individuals. The last rows explain why NGOs default to institutional funding, which is cheaper per rupee, and why that is dangerous: it hands your agenda to the funder.
notes.23: Donors give for several reasons and rarely only from altruism. Match each motive in the table to a response. The last row explains more giving than any other: being asked by someone they trust. That is why board introductions outperform cold approaches. Ask your own donors why they gave.
notes.24: Check your case for support against the five donor questions: why this cause, why this organisation, why now, why me and how will I know. The slide singles out 'why now' as the one most cases cannot answer. Without it, agreeing to give costs nothing and can be put off indefinitely.
notes.25: Restricted money is tied to a purpose, and unrestricted money is yours to allocate. An organisation can be fully funded and still unable to pay for an audit if all its income is restricted. Track the two separately in every board report.
notes.26: Money carries power. Each row pairs the party that decides with the party that knows. The slide calls this the structural fact of grant funding, with no blame on any particular funder. Some terms are negotiable, such as indicators, timelines and reporting rhythm, and grantees rarely test them.
notes.27: These are the four distortions the imbalance produces: chasing fashionable themes, reporting crowding out delivery, short cycles blocking long work and indicators shaping the programme. Each is a rational response to an incentive. Naming them is the first step to negotiating trust-based, flexible, multi-year funding.
notes.28: Check the donor as well. Before accepting money, ask where it comes from, what conditions attach and whether the community would object. Decide your red lines before an offer exists. The slide's warning for advocacy groups is that a grant limiting what you can say has bought your silence.
notes.29: Group donors into segments with different needs and channels, from the first-time giver to the institutional funder. The same appeal sent to all five underperforms on every segment. Segmentation needs five lists and five messages, so build it into the calendar.
notes.31: A strategy answers four questions: how much, from whom, by when and who is responsible. The last row of the table is what makes it a strategy, since it states what you will decline. Write down the funders and grant types you will not chase.
notes.32: Write the case for support once, well, and adapt it for each audience. It answers five things, from the problem to what happens if nobody acts. Test it on someone outside the sector. If they cannot repeat the problem and your response, the case is not working.
notes.33: Prospect research is the filter that saves months. Use the five checks: theme, geography, typical size, organisations like you and whether they are open. The size check is the most useful. A funder whose median grant is ₹5 lakh will not give ₹50 lakh however good the fit.
notes.34: The ask is one moment in a long cycle: identify, cultivate, ask, steward, renew. The two stages most often skipped are cultivation and stewardship, and they cost little and decide outcomes. An organisation that only identifies and asks runs a cold-approach operation at the worst conversion rate.
notes.35: Cultivation builds trust before the ask: updates with no ask, a site visit, questions about priorities and introductions to the community. The strongest signal is honesty about a setback. Set the date you will ask by, because cultivating forever is a way to avoid the discomfort of asking.
notes.36: Make the ask specific in amount, purpose and next step, then stop talking. Compare the weak and strong columns: 'whatever you can' against ₹12 lakh over two years. Ask for what the work costs, including a fair share of overheads. Filling the silence means negotiating against yourself.
notes.37: Stewardship is where the next gift is earned. Thank within days, confirm use, report results in full and stay in contact between asks. A mixed result reported in full is survivable, the slide says, and one the funder discovers later is not. Give stewardship to a named person.
notes.38: Read the pyramid from the base up: many small donors at the bottom, a few major and legacy donors at the top. The aim is to move people up over time. The slide says levels vary by organisation, so draw your own version with real numbers.
notes.40: Use the two tables as a proposal checklist. Each section answers one question and has a typical pitfall, such as activities mistaken for outcomes. The budget mismatch is the one reviewers spot fastest, so read your proposal backwards, from budget to activities to objectives.
notes.41: Open with the problem, and state who is affected, how badly and why it persists, with evidence. The third row, your analysis of why it persists locally, shows you know the place. Compare the weak and strong examples on the slide and rewrite your own opening.
notes.42: Objectives describe change. Use the table to classify statements as activity, output or outcome. Most rejected proposals fail between the output and outcome rows. Every objective needs a baseline, so budget the measurement. If you cannot say how you would measure it, it is not yet an objective.
notes.43: Memorise the five levels from inputs to impact. You control the first three, partly control outcomes and barely control impact, yet funders judge you on outcomes. Promise the outcome, state the impact it contributes to and say that other factors decide the rest.
notes.44: Outputs count what you produce and outcomes record what changes. The table gives three outputs, the outcome each should produce and how each can fail: wells break and kits get resold. Report outputs as outputs, and never call them impact.
notes.45: Each objective needs an indicator, a baseline, a target and a method, plus a budget line. The baseline cannot be added later, so collect it before any activity. Budget M&E explicitly, as the slide says, or it gets done badly at the end by whoever is free.
notes.46: Funders ask what happens when their money ends. Name a specific mechanism: community ownership, government adoption or earned income. The table marks 'we will seek further funding' as the default non-answer. If a benefit is permanent once delivered, such as an immunisation, say so plainly.
notes.47: Five craft rules, ranked by how cheaply they lose you the grant. Follow the format and word limits exactly, because exceeding them gets proposals rejected unread. Match budget and narrative line for line. Use plain language, and ask someone outside the sector to read it before you submit.
notes.49: The budget is your theory of change in money. Read the signals table as a reviewer would: round numbers read as estimated, no inflation reads as unconsidered and 3% overheads read as unsustainable. Avoid padding and under-budgeting, since under-budgeting to look competitive means delivering at a loss.
notes.50: Direct costs are tied to the project and indirect costs are shared. Funders readily fund the first and cap or question the second. The slide's advice is to calculate your true overhead rate once a year and state the basis, such as shared costs over total direct costs.
notes.51: Every overhead on the list is something the funder requires, and several funders will not pay for it. That contradiction is the whole argument. Name the item and its cost in conversation: 'the audit your grant requires costs ₹1.2 lakh' is harder to refuse than 'we need 15% overhead'.
notes.52: The starvation cycle needs both parties. Funders press for low overheads, NGOs under-report true cost, systems weaken, funders see weakness and press again. Individually, honesty can cost you grants. The slide's remedy is collective: sector bodies agreeing a common definition of true cost.
notes.53: The chart is illustrative, so use it for its direction. Acquiring new donors is expensive and keeping them is cheap, and the first gift rarely pays for itself, while the second and tenth do. Include the cost of fundraising in your own budget.
notes.54: Full cost recovery prices each project at its direct cost plus a fair share of overheads. The last row, willingness to decline, makes the rest real. Some strategic projects are worth taking at a loss, such as entering a new geography, but decide that deliberately and record it.
notes.55: Co-funding and matching differ. Co-funding means you bring a share of the budget, and matching multiplies what you raise elsewhere. Never commit co-funding you have not secured. Ask whether valued in-kind contributions count, since volunteer time or donated space may meet the requirement.
notes.56: Funders check reserves, audited accounts, the programme-to-cost ratio, cash flow and current registrations. An implausibly high programme ratio, such as 95%, is a red flag because overheads are probably hidden in programme lines. Registrations lapse without warning, so check yours regularly.
notes.58: Individual giving gives you unrestricted income, renewal by habit, independence, resilience and a constituency. The last row is worth more than money in a crisis: ten thousand donors notice if you are threatened, while three funders are only three. Starting late is normal. Never starting is the failure.
notes.59: The chart is illustrative: acquiring a donor costs far more than keeping one. The takeaway is allocation. Check how your own time and budget divide between finding new donors and keeping existing ones, because pouring everything into acquisition means running to stand still.
notes.60: Judge a donor by lifetime value instead of the first gift. A ₹500 monthly donor over ten years is worth far more than a one-off ₹5,000, and you can check it yourself with 500 × 12 × 10. Lifetime value justifies acquisition spend and makes retention the highest-return activity.
notes.61: The phrase doing the work is 'their specific gift'. A general impact report says what the organisation did, while naming what their ₹5,000 paid for tells them why to give again. Thank within days, show the impact within weeks and keep in touch between asks.
notes.62: Monthly donors give predictable income at low servicing cost with the highest retention, and the income is usually unrestricted. The only drawback is slow growth. Make cancelling easy and visible, because hard-to-cancel gifts produce complaints, chargebacks and reputational damage that outweigh the retained donations.
notes.63: Major donors need leadership time, personal cultivation, tailored proposals and bespoke reporting, so use the left column as a checklist. Organisations without a committed director or board rarely build this stream. Watch concentration: three donors providing most individual income is single-funder dependence in a different costume.
notes.64: Institutions respond to evidence and individuals respond to story, each in the right order. For individual appeals use one real story, told with dignity and consent, and lead with evidence for committees. Using the wrong approach loses the room either way. Section 11 covers the ethics.
notes.66: Section 135 of the Companies Act, 2013 turned corporate giving from discretion into a duty. That makes CSR predictable and changes your position: the company needs eligible partners to discharge its obligation. Use the before-and-after table as a short summary for colleagues.
notes.67: Qualifying companies must spend at least 2% of their average net profit over the preceding three financial years. Learn the five elements in the table. The slide tells you to confirm current thresholds in the Act and CSR Rules before advising anyone. Unspent-funds rules make the final quarter a better time to approach.
notes.68: Prospect CSR from the disclosures. Check whether Section 135 applies, what they spent, on which Schedule VII heads and where. The best signal is under-spend: a company that failed to spend last year is under pressure to place funds this year. Companies with operations in your district are better prospects.
notes.69: CSR money can only go to Schedule VII activities. If your project does not map to a head, a company cannot fund it, so frame proposals to fit the schedule explicitly. CSR cannot fund your organisation's core costs, which is why it does not solve the unrestricted-income problem.
notes.70: CSR-1 is an eligibility gate. Without it a company generally cannot route CSR money to you, however well you fit. Learn the four registrations in the table and get them in place before you approach companies. Registration takes time, and the conversation usually ends when the gap surfaces.
notes.71: This chart is illustrative and shows no official data. It suggests education and health attract large shares of CSR, but the slide tells you to confirm current patterns from published CSR data before relying on them. Treat it as a prompt to check a company's own disclosure.
notes.72: Companies answer to a board and to public disclosure, so they look for valid registrations, a verifiable track record, rigorous reporting, alignment with their theme and outcomes they can report. Offer a site visit early, because companies fund what they have seen.
notes.73: Read this as five constraints and their consequences. Schedule VII means no core funding, the March cycle makes timing matter and companies prefer visible projects. Decide your co-branding position before the first conversation. Being ready with a good proposal in January is an advantage.
notes.75: Compliance makes fundraising possible. Each registration unlocks something, from untaxed income to CSR funds and foreign contributions. The disclaimer matters: this is an orientation, so confirm with a professional and the current statute. The last row catches established organisations whose filings lapse.
notes.76: 12A exempts the NGO's income from tax provided it is applied to charitable objects. The move to 12AB made registration renewable, so diarise renewal dates well ahead. The slide also gives the section number in the Income-tax Act 2025 from 1 April 2026 beside the older reference.
notes.77: 80G benefits the donor, who can claim a deduction. Put your 80G status on the donation page, receipt and appeal, because donors who cannot tell whether a gift is deductible tend to assume it is not. Issue receipts promptly and with the prescribed details.
notes.78: Remember the pairing: 12A protects the NGO's income, and 80G makes giving cheaper for the donor. Most NGOs pursue both together. For fundraising, 80G is the competitive asset, since organisations without it are at a disadvantage they often do not notice.
notes.79: FCRA governs foreign contributions, and getting it wrong is a legal problem. Learn the five requirements in the table, including valid registration, the designated SBI New Delhi account and the ban on sub-granting. If foreign funding is material, name it as a risk in your diversification plan.
notes.80: The 2020 amendment made two changes fundraisers must know: no sub-granting of foreign funds, and receipt only in the designated SBI New Delhi account. The first reshaped intermediary models and many small organisations lost their route. Take legal advice before you restructure any partnership that relied on passing funds on.
notes.81: Compliance satisfies the regulator and transparency earns trust. Publish audited accounts and an annual report on your website, report failures as well as successes and answer to communities. Voluntary disclosure is rare, so it works as a differentiator with donors comparing options.
notes.82: Keep one compliance calendar with a named owner and reminders months ahead. The table shows what each missed date costs, from FCRA renewal risk to a CSR partner who cannot close its own reporting. Almost every compliance failure is a missed date, and the fourth row costs you the relationship.
notes.84: Calculate the share of income from your largest funder and put it in every board pack. The slide's bands are over 70% as one decision from crisis and 40–70% as vulnerable. Note that the bands skip 30–40%, so check where your figure falls before you rely on them.
notes.85: Diversification trades a little efficiency for a lot of resilience. The timelines run from a year for a second institutional funder to three years for a monthly base. Every timeline is longer than the crisis that prompts the decision, so start while things are fine.
notes.86: There are two failure modes. Too concentrated is catastrophic the day a funder leaves, and too scattered means dozens of small grants whose reporting burden swallows the organisation. The scattered case looks like diversification. Set a floor on grant size relative to its administrative burden.
notes.87: Reserves buy time: to survive a delayed tranche, replace a lost funder, pre-finance contracts and decline bad money. The last benefit is the most underrated. Reserves can only come from unrestricted income, which is why starting individual giving is worth the slow return.
notes.88: Unrestricted income is the truest measure of financial freedom, and none of its sources is easy. Set an explicit target for the unrestricted share and grow it yearly. The slide's practical tip is to ask existing funders for a share unrestricted. More will say yes than you expect.
notes.89: Earned income gives control, but the accounting often hides the cost. Earned-income arms look profitable because programme staff time is never charged to them. Cost each stream in full at staff rates. An activity that would lose money if costed properly is being subsidised by grants.
notes.90: Follow the five steps: map, target, invest, sequence, review. The map produces the concentration ratio and the restricted-unrestricted split. Build one new stream at a time, since starting individual giving, earned income and CSR together usually builds none. Fund the investment explicitly.
notes.91: Sustainability is bigger than money: capable staff, working systems, community ownership and a clear mission. The test on the slide is what survives your departure. If relationships, knowledge and systems live in individuals, the organisation is one resignation from a crisis no grant will fix.
notes.93: Stories carry power over the people in them. Tell them with dignity: the person is an agent, has chosen to be in it, can decline, is named as they wish and is accurately portrayed. The slide flags composite stories as misrepresentation unless labelled, so say so if you use one.
notes.94: Poverty porn works in the short term, which is why it persists. The table gives the dignified alternative to each feature. The practical test is whether you would be comfortable showing the material to the person in it, in front of their neighbours. If you would not, do not publish.
notes.95: Consent means comprehension, and a form alone does not prove it. It must cover where the story appears, how long, the right to withdraw and whether the person is named. The last row matters most: refusal must cost them nothing. Ask through someone with no power over the person.
notes.96: Upward accountability to donors is enforced by money, and downward accountability to communities has no enforcement. So the second needs a deliberate mechanism, such as feedback, published budgets or a grievance route. The slide's test: does the community know what the project cost and what it was meant to achieve?
notes.97: Five lines a fundraiser should not cross, from misleading claims to unconsented stories. Decide them before you are under pressure, because a line gets tested when crossing it funds three salaries. Write them into a fundraising policy the board has approved.
notes.98: Five takeaways, each paired with the failure it prevents. The slide's advice is to take one number from the whole deck: the share of income from your largest funder. Calculate it this week. Then check your compliance gates, because a missing CSR-1 or a lapsed 80G removes you from consideration.
notes.99: Read primary sources for anything compliance-related, since summaries of CSR and FCRA go out of date. The table lists the Companies Act, the FCRA, the Income-tax Act 2025, NGO Darpan and MCA portals. The last row is your own audited accounts, where the concentration ratio and unrestricted share live. Start there.
